sections.title: Types of media
sections.content:
Vocabulary for discussing modern media:
• broadcast — transmit a programme on TV or radio. The event was broadcast live to millions of viewers.
• tabloid — a newspaper focusing on sensational stories. Tabloids often exaggerate stories for dramatic effect.
• editorial — an article giving the newspaper's opinion. The editorial criticised the government's new policy.
• podcast — a digital audio programme available online. She hosts a popular podcast on language learning.
• correspondent — a journalist reporting from a particular place. Our foreign correspondent filed a report from the war zone.

sections.title: Media influence
sections.content:
How media shapes public perception:
• bias — unfair prejudice in reporting. Readers should be aware of political bias in the news.
• propaganda — misleading information to promote a viewpoint. Propaganda was widely used during wartime.
• sensationalism — exaggerating news for excitement. Sensationalism in the media undermines public trust.
• misinformation — false information spread unintentionally. Misinformation on social media spreads rapidly.
• censorship — suppressing information considered harmful. Internet censorship restricts access to information in some countries.

exercises.question: Unfair prejudice for or against something in reporting is:
exercises.explanation: Bias is prejudice in favour of or against one thing compared to another, usually unfairly.

exercises.question: Exaggerating news stories to make them more exciting is:
exercises.hint: Making stories bigger than they are.
exercises.explanation: Sensationalism is presenting stories in a way that provokes public interest at the expense of accuracy.

exercises.question: False information spread without intent to deceive is:
exercises.hint: Not deliberate lying, but still wrong.
exercises.explanation: Misinformation is false or inaccurate information, especially that spread unintentionally.

exercises.question: A journalist who reports from a specific location or country is a:
exercises.explanation: A correspondent is a journalist reporting from a particular area or on a particular topic.

exercises.question: The official suppression of information or expression is:
exercises.explanation: Censorship is the suppression of speech, communication, or information deemed objectionable.

exercises.question: A newspaper known for dramatic, less serious stories is a:
exercises.hint: Often has large headlines and celebrity gossip.
exercises.explanation: A tabloid is a newspaper with short articles and lots of pictures, focusing on sensational content.

exercises.question: Misleading information used to promote a political cause is:
exercises.explanation: Propaganda is information used to promote a political cause or point of view, often misleadingly.

exercises.question: An article expressing the newspaper's own official opinion is an:
exercises.explanation: An editorial is a newspaper article expressing the editor's opinion on a topical issue.
